claim: The same 1,000 YouTube views at the same 70% ad-inventory fill yields roughly INR 30 (under USD 1) when the audience is Indian versus USD 5 when the audience is American or from another developed country — a five-to-sixfold revenue gap driven purely by audience geography.
stance_target: Creator income figures derived from US/Western audiences cannot be transferred to Global South or Southeast Asian markets; the same audience size produces roughly a fifth to a sixth of the revenue.
scope_conditions: Single-informant figure from Ajay Gupta, CEO of Broccoli Animation, an Indian animation studio producing crime/horror content FOR a US audience. Genre-specific ('in my genre'). Interview conducted within the 2017-2023 fieldwork window. Not a platform-audited figure and not a sample statistic — treat as a practitioner-reported order of magnitude, corroborated in direction by the Turkish CPM evidence in the same paper.
quoted_support: 1000 views with 70% or more inventory fill (of advertisements) would translate to roughly INR 30 (less than 1 US $) in my genre if the views came from the Indian audience. The same views and inventory fill percentage would lead to USD 5 if the views come from the U.S. or any other developed country.
region: India vs United States. NON-WESTERN evidence — the closest available analogue for Southeast Asian monetization, but India is not Southeast Asia.

claim: A Turkish production house's kids channel received 10% of its views from Germany but 30% of its income from Germany, a threefold income-per-view premium for a high-CPM Western audience.
stance_target: Audience geography, not audience size, is the dominant determinant of creator revenue outside high-CPM Western markets.
scope_conditions: Reported by 'Can', manager of production house PH-1, Turkey; interviews Dec 2019 - Jun 2020. Single channel, kids genre. Practitioner-reported channel analytics, not independently audited.
quoted_support: on our kids' channel, 10% of the views were from Germany, but 30% of the income was coming from Germany. . . . Since the CPM is higher there, [you would earn] more for less views.
region: Turkey / Germany — non-Western creator, Western audience

claim: Six of seven Irish YouTube creators interviewed could not generate a livable income from YouTube and depended on full-time or freelance jobs; only one, who had previously worked in a production house, could.
stance_target: Even in an English-speaking, high-income Western country, the large majority of interviewed creators cannot earn a living wage from the platform.
scope_conditions: n=7 Irish creators, interviewed November 2019 - June 2020, recruited by purposive and snowball sampling. Sample far too small and non-random to estimate a population rate; this is a within-sample count, not a prevalence estimate. Pre-dates the 2021-2023 monetization changes.
quoted_support: At the time of the research, none of the Irish participants, except one who used to work in a production house (PH), were able to generate a livable income from YouTube media production. Thus, six of the Irish creators were aspirational and had other income sources coming from their full-time or freelance jobs.
numbers: 6 of 7 (85.7%) not earning a livable income
region: Ireland — WESTERN, English-language; generalizes poorly to Southeast Asia in both directions

claim: All nine Turkish participants earned a sustainable full-time income from YouTube, but seven of the nine worked inside a production house rather than as independent creators.
stance_target: That apparent creator-income success in a non-Western market reflects viable solo creator careers rather than institutional employment.
scope_conditions: n=9 Turkish participants, December 2019 - June 2020, purposive and snowball sampling explicitly weighted toward professionals. Selection into the sample is on the outcome (professionalized creators), so the 9-of-9 figure is a sampling artefact, not a survival rate.
quoted_support: At the time of the research, all Turkish participants were making a sustainable full-time income from YouTube media production. While two of them were independent creators, seven of them were working in the context of a PH with different and sometimes multiple titles such as a manager, a founder, a content editor, a director, a production manager, a content head, and a YouTube creator.

claim: 66% of YouTube's top 250 channels produce English-language content, followed by Spanish at 15% and Portuguese at 7%, structurally disadvantaging creators working in other languages.
stance_target: Language market size is a structural, measurable constraint on creator income ceilings outside the anglophone core — directly relevant to Thai-language and other Southeast Asian creators.
scope_conditions: Cited secondhand from Gomez (2023) within the Bidav & Mehta article; original methodology not verified. Top 250 channels only — an elite tail, not the full channel population.
quoted_support: Given that 66% of YouTube's top 250 channels produce English-language content, followed by Spanish (15%) and Portuguese (7%) languages (Gomez, 2023) and YouTube's Cost Per Mile (CPM) . . . revenue is relatively lower in India, Ireland, and Turkey compared with more lucrative advertising markets like the United States and United Kingdom

claim: Turkish production houses set brand-deal thresholds at guaranteed view counts — one guarantees 500,000 video views to partners, another relies on 1-4 million views per video.
stance_target: Quantifies the audience scale required to access non-advertising creator revenue in a mid-size non-English language market.
scope_conditions: Two production houses in Turkey (PH-1 and PH-2), interviewed Dec 2019 - Jun 2020. Production-house scale, not individual-creator scale.
quoted_support: Turkish participant Can, manager of PH-1, for example, mentions that his company guarantees 500 K video views to potential partners, whereas the PH-2's channel for which Turkish participant Yigit works relies on the high number of video views like 1-4M views in brand deals.

claim: Indian creators earning YouTube revenue from foreign audiences face 25-30% corporate tax on net income between 10 million and 100 million INR plus a 20% foreign-remittance levy, raised from 5% in 2023.
stance_target: Gross platform revenue overstates net creator income in non-Western jurisdictions, widening the effective geographic income gap beyond the CPM differential alone.
scope_conditions: Cited from PwC Worldwide Tax Summaries (2023) and Das (2023). Applies to incorporated creator businesses in India above the 10M INR threshold, not to individual small creators.
quoted_support: It is important to understand here that the Government of India levies between 25% and 30% corporate tax on a net income between 10 M and 100 M INR (PwC Worldwide Tax Summaries, 2023). This is followed by an additional 20% (raised from 5% in 2023) on foreign remittance (Das, 2023).

claim: In Turkey, 4 of the 10 most-watched YouTube channels belong to legacy media companies and 5 are kids-content channels, leaving essentially one slot in the national top ten for an independent adult-content creator.
stance_target: In smaller non-English language markets, the top of the attention distribution is occupied by incumbent media firms and a single high-volume genre, compressing the opportunity available to independent creators.
scope_conditions: Cited secondhand from Yakar (2023) within the article; original methodology and measurement window not verified. Turkey only.
quoted_support: this competition increases even more considering that 4 of the 10 most watched YouTube channels in Turkey belong to the legacy media and 5 are kids content channels, highlighting the importance of genre in generating significant income (Yakar, 2023).
